newsitem.title: USA: Senate spy panel chief says may oppose CIA nominee.
newsitem.headline: Senate spy panel chief says may oppose CIA nominee.

text.p: The Senate Intelligence Committee chairman voiced "great reservations" on Wednesday about confirming Anthony Lake, President Bill Clinton's choice to run the troubled Central Intelligence Agency, because of a secret diplomatic move that misled Congress on Bosnia.

In a new sign that a confirmation battle may be brewing, Sen. Arlen Specter, a Pennsylvania Republican, said he might oppose Lake, currently Clinton's national security adviser, over a 1994 policy on Iranian arms shipments that kept both Congress and then-CIA director James Woolsey in the dark.
"I have great reservations about Mr. Lake and about his sensitivity given what went on in this matter," Specter said at a final hearing for outgoing CIA chief John Deutch.

Specter was the second senior Republican senator in a week to question Lake's nomination. Pete Domenici, of New Mexico, said Sunday Lake faced "tough sailing" in the Senate and called his replacement of Deutch "a kind of in-house coup."
But White House spokesman Mike McCurry played down the possiblity that Lake's Iran-Bosnia gambit might pose a hurdle, saying the issue had been thoroughly reviewed.

"I think the items of concern there have been addressed by the administration and addressed by Mr. Lake on other occasions," McCurry said. "I am not aware that that should pose any significant problem..."
As national security adviser, Lake was an architect of a policy that gave Croatia a secret green light to let Iranian arms reach beleaguered Bosnian Moslems in violation of a U.N. embargo.

The intelligence committee, which is to hold the first vote on Lake, said in a report last month that Lake, along with Deputy Secretary of State Strobe Talbott, intentionally misled Congress and Woolsey, Clinton's first CIA director, about the decision to support Iranian arms shipments.

Specter said he would vote against confirmation if Lake maintained that as director of central intelligence he could withhold such secrets from the intelligence oversight panels, set up in 1975 to watch over U.S. spy agencies.

"It would make it an easy question for me to vote no on his confirmation," Specter said. He compared Lake's handling of the Bosnia arms issue to the bypassing of Congress that was at the heart of the Iran-Contra scandal, the worst foreign policy problem of President Ronald Reagan's administration.

Committee Vice Chairman Bob Kerrey, a Nebraska Democrat, joined several of his colleagues in regretting the departure of Deutch, whom he described as a courageous, tough-minded manager who would be "sorely missed."
"I wish you were staying," Kerrey told Deutch, whom Clinton decided to dump after 20 months as part of his revamped second-term national security team. Kerrey said he meant no "disrespect" to Lake.

Republican qualms about Lake emerged on Sunday when Sen. Pete Domenici of New Mexico predicted that of Clinton's four new choices for top foreign policy jobs the CIA nominee would be the one to face "tough sailing" on Capitol Hill.

Domenici was joined in raising doubts about Lake by former Secretary of State Lawrence Eagleburger and by Woolsey, who was squeezed out in early 1995 after running afoul of Congress over Aldrich Ames, the CIA veteran convicted in 1994 of spying for Moscow for nine years.

Eagleburger wondered if Lake, who shuns the limelight, was "strong enough" to continue reforms at the CIA, which he said was in "bad shape." Woolsey, who endorsed Republican Bob Dole for president this year, said Lake may find it "hard (but) not impossible" to pass on CIA analysis that reflects ill on foreign policies Lake helped craft as Clinton's point man.

Deutch, in his testimony, voiced confidence that Lake would be an excellent successor and said he had his full support. He said he hoped Lake, once confirmed, would stay at the job for Clinton's entire second term.
